entities.name: St. Cecilia's Abbey, Solesmes
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Saint-Cécile de Solesmes Abbey (Abbaye Saint-Cécile de Solesmes), a Benedictine women's monastery in Solesmes, Sarthe, France — the female counterpart community to the famous Saint-Pierre de Solesmes Abbey (founded 1010) and directly associated with Solesmes's world-renowned Gregorian chant research and performance tradition — was established in 1866 as the first new women's Benedictine community in France after the French Revolution's destruction of most religious houses, under the direction of Dom Prosper Guéranger, the pivotal figure in the 19th-century Gregorian chant revival.

Saint-Cécile's founding by Guéranger in 1866 placed it at the center of the Solesmes Gregorian chant movement — one of the most important developments in the history of Catholic sacred music. Guéranger's Solesmes community had been systematically researching, reconstructing, and performing authentic medieval Gregorian chant since the 1830s, arguing that the corrupt and embellished 17th-18th century Baroque chant editions should be replaced by the medieval originals. This work produced the Solesmes school of chant paleography and performance practice that ultimately shaped the 1903 Motu Proprio of Pope Pius X, which established Gregorian chant as the official music of the Catholic Church's liturgy and explicitly cited the Solesmes research.

The women's community at Saint-Cécile participates in the same Gregorian chant tradition as Saint-Pierre. The Solesmes Abbey's chant research and the Éditions de Solesmes publications have shaped Catholic liturgical music worldwide. Saint-Cécile de Solesmes continues as an active Benedictine women's community and is internationally recognized for its chant.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Saint-Cécile de Solesmes Abbey — participating in the Gregorian chant revival that shaped Catholic liturgical music worldwide, founded by the pivotal Dom Guéranger, and continuing as an active Benedictine women's community — is historically significant as part of the Solesmes tradition that permanently transformed the Catholic Church's musical heritage.
